title: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
lead: Housing testers receive different vacancy answers according to race. Their suit separates injury to a right to truthful information from neighborhood and organizational injuries, and then separates standing from timely filing.

actors.name: Havens Realty Corporation and Rose Jones
actors.role: Owner of two apartment complexes and its employee, accused of racial steering.

actors.name: Sylvia Coleman and R. Kent Willis
actors.role: Black and white housing testers employed by HOME.

actors.name: Housing Opportunities Made Equal (HOME)
actors.role: Housing counseling and referral organization alleging impairment of its own work.

actors.name: Paul Coles
actors.role: Black prospective renter whose separate claims proceeded to trial and settlement.

proceedings: The district court dismissed Coleman, Willis, and HOME before discovery; Coles’s separate case proceeded to findings and a consent order.
The Fourth Circuit reinstated the dismissed claims.
The Supreme Court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded for proceedings consistent with its distinct standing and limitations rulings.
limits: This is a historical transformation of the canonical brief, not a fresh audit or statement of present statutory deadlines. The 180-day period was the rule then applied. Allegations supporting standing were not final merits findings; the Court did not review Coles’s separate merits judgment or decide HOME’s associational standing.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Testers and a prospective renter receive conflicting vacancy information
sections.cue: Who claimed a personal consequence from the alleged steering?
paragraphs: Havens Realty Corporation owned and operated Camelot Townhouses and Colonial Court Apartments in Henrico County near Richmond, Virginia. Its employee Rose Jones handled rental inquiries. Housing Opportunities Made Equal, known as HOME, employed Sylvia Coleman, who was Black, and R. Kent Willis, who was white, as testers. They posed as applicants to investigate discrimination, without intending to rent.

On three dates in March 1978, Coleman allegedly was told no apartments were available while Willis was told vacancies existed. On July 6, Coleman again was told Camelot had no vacancies, while a different white tester received contrary information. On July 13, Paul Coles, a Black prospective renter, allegedly was falsely told Camelot had no apartments and directed toward integrated Colonial Court.

The January 1979 complaint accused Havens and Jones of racial steering designed to preserve segregation. The individuals alleged loss of benefits from integrated communities. HOME, which counseled housing seekers and investigated and referred discrimination complaints, alleged that the practices impaired those services and drained its resources.

sections.title: Dismissal and a separate settlement create two litigation paths
sections.cue: Why was there still a live controversy?
paragraphs: Before discovery or evidence, the district court dismissed Coleman, Willis, and HOME for lack of standing and expiration of the then-applicable 180-day filing period. Coles’s claims remained, went to trial, and produced an unlawful-steering finding followed by a consent order providing monetary and injunctive relief to him and his class. The Fourth Circuit reversed the other dismissals, accepting standing allegations and treating the practice as continuing through Coles’s timely incident.

The dismissed plaintiffs conditionally agreed with the defendants that, if the district court approved, each would receive $400 and no further relief if Supreme Court review was denied or the judgment affirmed, but nothing if reversed. Justice Brennan’s unanimous Supreme Court opinion held that arrangement did not moot the appeal. It merely fixed potential damages contingent on the outcome; adverse claims remained, and these plaintiffs could not recover from Coles’s separate fund. The Court did not review the correctness of his merits determination.

sections.title: Coleman alleges injury to a statutory information right
sections.cue: Why did the white tester have a different result?
paragraphs: The Court’s Gladstone precedent understood the Fair Housing Act’s private enforcement provision to reach Article III’s limits, without an additional prudential barrier. A plaintiff still needed distinct, palpable injury caused by the defendants. A statutory right could identify that injury, but did not abolish the requirement.

Section 804(d) prohibited racially discriminatory statements to any person that an available dwelling was unavailable. Coleman alleged that very invasion of her own right to truthful information. Her expectation of discrimination and investigative purpose did not erase it. Unlike the Act’s refusal-to-rent provision, this language did not require a bona fide offer.

Willis alleged accurate vacancy information. He neither alleged injury to this information right nor pleaded a discriminatory-misrepresentation cause of action. His role as a tester therefore did not itself establish standing.

sections.title: Neighborhood allegations need development, while HOME alleges direct impairment
sections.cue: Which injuries could still be substantiated?
paragraphs: Coleman and Willis separately alleged lost social, professional, economic, political, and aesthetic benefits of integrated neighborhoods. Those could be personal injuries even when steering directly violated someone else’s statutory rights, provided their own harm was fairly traceable to it.

Their allegations were nevertheless strikingly vague. Living somewhere in Richmond or Henrico County did not explain how discrimination at two adjacent complexes affected their neighborhoods. Metropolitan-wide effects were implausible, and prior cases involved relatively compact areas. Still, the Court could not exclude an appreciable local effect before development. On remand, the district court had to permit more definite allegations and dismiss if the resulting record still failed to establish standing.

HOME alleged perceptible impairment of its counseling and referral services and a consequent resource drain. That was concrete organizational injury beyond frustration of an abstract mission. It would have to prove impairment to obtain relief, but dismissal on these allegations was improper. Because HOME appeared willing to abandon a separate representative claim for injunctions, the Court left associational standing undecided.

sections.title: The filing deadline defeats Coleman’s otherwise cognizable tester claim
sections.cue: What survived the Supreme Court’s judgment?
paragraphs: Under the Act’s then-existing 180-day period, a continuing unlawful practice extending into the filing window differed from an isolated stale act. The neighborhood and organizational injuries allegedly flowed from an ongoing pattern including Coles’s July 13 incident, so those claims survived limitations dismissal. The Attorney General’s pattern-or-practice authority did not reserve such claims exclusively to public enforcement.

Coleman personally received misinformation on four discrete occasions, all outside 180 days. Later misinformation to Coles did not invade her information right. Her tester claim was untimely despite sufficient injury; Willis’s failed because he received no misinformation.

On February 24, 1982, the Court affirmed reinstatement of the neighborhood and HOME organizational claims, reversed permission for the two tester claims to proceed, and directed consistent proceedings on remand. It awarded no damages. Justice Powell joined but separately criticized nearly four years of litigation without meaningful neighborhood facts. Amendment or a more definite statement should have been required earlier; because proper procedural preconditions to dismissal had not been observed, he agreed the Court could not dismiss those claims now.
